To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Bayes-optima error of a given problem is bounded from below as a function of the geometry of class-conditional data distributions and the noise corruption rate.

(1) The Bayes-optimal adversarial attack is a simple algorithm based optimal transport, (2) The adversarial error of classifiers can be computed via the geometry of the underlying class-conditional densities, (3) Robustness to random noise is governed by a nonlinear data-processing inequality.

(1) the adversarial attack that maximally increases the error of a classifier is an optimal transport plan, which can be computed via an algorithm that is simple and efficient; (2) adversarial attacks can increase error of classifiers beyond the Bayes-optimum, which can be explained via a simple data-processing inequality; (3) random noise corruption of examples can be explained as an instance of the data-processing inequality; and (4) our lower-bounds for adversarial and noisy attacks are universal
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following fundamental question: how much can a classifier be expected to generalize in the presence of noise or adversarial attacks?
the theoretical limits of classification under adversarial attacks and random noise corruption.
the fundamental limits of robustness in classification, and our work provides a theoretical foundation for the design of robust classifiers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Bayes-optimum error of a classifier is lower-bounded by the error it makes on clean test data, plus an additional term that is determined by the geometry of the data, and the corruption model.

the Bayes-optimum error under random corruptions is always greater than or equal to the Bayes-optium error under adversarial corruptions, which in turn is greater than or equal the ordinary test error.
the robustness to test time attacks is a function of the data geometry, and not the classifier.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, for any classification problem with a given geometry of the data distributions, there exist a lower-bound on the test-error of any classifier.

we derive lower-bounds for the Bayes-error of classifiers under adversarial attacks, and noisy corruptions, which are independent of the classifier and depend only on the geometry of class-conditional distributions.
the Bayes-optimum error is lower-bounded by the error under adversarial attacks and noise corruption.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the robustness to adversarial attacks and random noise is fundamentally limited by the geometry of the problem.
the Bayes-optimum error under adversarial attacks and random corruption is fundamentally linked to the geometry of class-conditional distributions.
the adversarial and noisy robustness limits are universal, i.e., independent of the classifier used for classification.
